content: Bordetella pertussis is a Gram-negative bacterium that is aerobic, non-motile, and does not form spores. It has a coccobacillus shape. This organism is the causative agent of pertussis, commonly known as whooping cough. Unlike Bordetella bronchiseptica, Bordetella pertussis lacks motility. Humans are the sole known reservoir for this pathogen. The outer membrane of Bordetella pertussis contains lipopolysaccharides (LPS) with a unique phosphate composition that distinguishes it from the LPS found in other bacterial species. Specifically, the outer membrane contains lipid X instead of lipid A, which is typically found in other bacterial lipopolysaccharides. This unique feature of the outer membrane is a defining characteristic of Bordetella pertussis. Taxonomically, Bordetella pertussis belongs to the kingdom Bacteria, phylum Proteobacteria, class Betaproteobacteria, order Burkholderiales, family Alcaligenaceae, genus Bordetella, and species pertussis. The genome of Bordetella pertussis consists of a single circular chromosome and plasmids. The circular chromosome contains 3,867 genes and 4,086,189 nucleotides. Additionally, the IncP-1 beta plasmid, known as pBP136, carries 46 open reading frames (ORFs) and contains 41,268 base pairs of nucleotides. Structurally, Bordetella pertussis has an outer membrane, an inner membrane, and a periplasmic space located between these two membranes. The rough lipopolysaccharide (also referred to as lipooligosaccharide) on the outer membrane contains lipid X, which is distinct from the lipid A found in other bacterial lipopolysaccharides. This unique composition of the outer membrane is a hallmark feature of Bordetella pertussis.
